For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(F_n\) be the free group on \(n\) generators. For any group \(G\), define its lower central series by \(\gamma_1(G)=G\) and \(\gamma_{r+1}(G)=[\gamma_r(G),G]\), where \([H,K]\) is the subgroup generated by the commutators \([h,k]=hkh^{-1}k^{-1}\) with \(h\in H\) and \(k\in K\). For every integer \(r\ge1\), define
\[
\mathcal A_r(n)=\ker\!\left(\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}\bigl(F_n/\gamma_{r+1}(F_n)\bigr)\right),
\qquad \operatorname{IA}_n=\mathcal A_1(n).
\]
Determine, by explicit conditions on \(n\) and \(c\), the complete set
\[
\mathcal D=\left\{(n,c)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\ 
\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)\subsetneq
\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)
\right\}.
\]

content.text:
This asks for a classification that is **not currently known**: it is a graded form of the Andreadakis problem.

To see the connection, put \(H=F_n/\gamma_2(F_n)\). The degree-\(c\) Johnson homomorphism restricts to a map
\[
J_c:\frac{\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)}
{\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)}
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}
\left(H,\frac{\gamma_{c+1}(F_n)}{\gamma_{c+2}(F_n)}\right).
\]
Here one uses the standard inclusion
\(\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\subseteq\mathcal A_c(n)\).
Its kernel is exactly
\[
\ker J_c=
\frac{\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)}
{\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(n,c)\in\mathcal D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J_c
\text{ is not injective}.
\]
The noninjectivity degrees of these maps have not been completely classified.

Some established facts illustrate the situation:

* **Rank two:** \(\operatorname{IA}_2=\operatorname{Inn}(F_2)\), and its lower central series agrees with the Andreadakis filtration. Thus
  \[
  (2,c)\notin\mathcal D\qquad(c\ge1).
  \]
* **Degree one:** the abelianization theorem for \(\operatorname{IA}_n\) gives
  \[
  \mathcal A_2(n)=[\operatorname{IA}_n,\operatorname{IA}_n],
  \]
  so \((n,1)\notin\mathcal D\).
* **A known counterexample:** Bartholdi’s rank-three computation gives a nonzero degree-six kernel, yielding
  \[
  (3,6)\in\mathcal D.
  \]

Moreover, if for a fixed \(n\) none of the pairs \((n,c)\) belonged to \(\mathcal D\), induction would give
\(\mathcal A_c(n)=\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\) for every \(c\): whenever equality holds at degree \(c\), absence from \(\mathcal D\) gives equality at degree \(c+1\).

Thus the requested complete explicit conditions go beyond the known results:
\[
\boxed{\text{A complete determination of }\mathcal D\text{ is an open problem.}}
\]

# Filtered-group countermodels: G = UT_{d+1}(F_3), 1 <= d <= 6.
# Its lower central series C has |C_r| = 3^((d+1-r)(d+2-r)/2)
# for r <= d and C_r=1 otherwise. Its last term C_d has order 3.
# Define A_r=C_r for r<=d, A_r=C_d for d<r<=7, A_r=1 for r>=8.
# The delayed term is central, so this is a strongly central filtration.
def clog(d, r):
    return (d+1-r)*(d+2-r)//2 if r <= d else 0

def alog(d, r):
    return clog(d, r) if r <= d else (1 if r <= 7 else 0)

for d in range(1,7):
    # Since all terms are nested C-series terms, log-order of an
    # intersection is the smaller log-order.
    kernels = [r for r in range(1,8)
               if min(clog(d,r), alog(d,r+1)) > clog(d,r+1)]
    cokernel7 = alog(d,7) - max(clog(d,7), alog(d,8))
    print(f'class {d}: nonzero kernel degrees {kernels}; degree-7 cokernel order {3**cokernel7}')

Here is a proof, including a uniform family of witnesses for strictness.

## 1. The graded Johnson maps

Write \(H=F_n^{\mathrm{ab}}\) and \(L_r=\gamma_r(F_n)/\gamma_{r+1}(F_n)\). Strong centrality of the Andreadakis filtration gives
\[
[\mathcal A_r(n),\mathcal A_s(n)]\subseteq\mathcal A_{r+s}(n),
\qquad
\gamma_r(\operatorname{IA}_n)\subseteq\mathcal A_r(n).
\]
Consequently the Johnson homomorphism induces
\[
J_c:\frac{\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)}
{\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)}
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H,L_{c+1}),
\]
whose kernel is precisely
\[
\ker J_c=
\frac{\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)}
{\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)}.
\tag{1}
\]

## 2. The equality cases

For \(c=1\), Magnus generation and the first Johnson homomorphism give
\[
\operatorname{IA}_n^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H^*\otimes\Lambda^2H.
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathcal A_2(n)=\gamma_2(\operatorname{IA}_n).
\]

For \(c=2\), use the integral degree-two Johnson injectivity theorem:
\[
J_2:\frac{\gamma_2(\operatorname{IA}_n)}
{\gamma_3(\operatorname{IA}_n)}
\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H,L_3).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\mathcal A_3(n)=\gamma_3(\operatorname{IA}_n).
\]
Thus no pair with \(c\le2\) belongs to \(\mathcal D\).

For rank two, Nielsen’s theorem gives
\[
\operatorname{IA}_2=\operatorname{Inn}(F_2)\cong F_2.
\]
The center formula for free nilpotent groups,
\[
Z(F_2/\gamma_{r+1}(F_2))
=\gamma_r(F_2)/\gamma_{r+1}(F_2),
\]
then implies
\[
\mathcal A_r(2)=\operatorname{Inn}(\gamma_r(F_2))
=\gamma_r(\operatorname{IA}_2).
\]
Hence no pair with \(n=2\) belongs to \(\mathcal D\).

## 3. Uniform witnesses for \(n\ge3,\ c\ge3\)

Use three of the free generators, denoted \(x,y,z\), and define automorphisms fixing all unmentioned generators by
\[
D:x\mapsto yxy^{-1},\qquad
A:x\mapsto[y,z]x,\qquad
B:z\mapsto[x,y]z.
\]
Put
\[
B_k=\operatorname{ad}_D^k(B),\qquad
\operatorname{ad}_D(g)=[D,g],
\]
and, for \(c\ge3\), set
\[
w_c=[D,[A,B_{c-3}]].
\tag{2}
\]
Plainly \(w_c\in\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\).

We first show that \(w_c\in\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)\). In the free Lie ring, write \(X,Y,Z\) for the initial forms of \(x,y,z\), and put \(T=\operatorname{ad}Y\). The first Johnson derivations of \(D,A,B\) are
\[
D(X)=TX,\qquad A(X)=TZ,\qquad B(Z)=-TX,
\]
with their other values zero. Therefore
\[
(\operatorname{ad}_D^kB)(Z)=-T^{k+1}X.
\]
The derivation \([A,\operatorname{ad}_D^kB]\) sends
\[
X\longmapsto T^{k+2}X,\qquad
Z\longmapsto -T^{k+2}Z,\qquad Y\longmapsto0.
\]
It commutes with \(D\). Since Johnson homomorphisms respect brackets,
\[
J_c(w_c)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
w_c\in\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n).
\tag{3}
\]

The remaining issue is nonmembership in \(\gamma_{c+1}\). For completeness, the integral detector is described next.

## 4. A stable integral detector

Let \(R=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]\), \(s=t-1\), and take the character
\[
F_n\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad y\longmapsto1,
\quad x_i\longmapsto0\quad(x_i\ne y).
\]
If \(N\) is its kernel, then \(N^{\mathrm{ab}}\) is a free \(R\)-module of rank \(n-1\). Every IA-automorphism acts \(R\)-linearly on it. This gives an Alexander representation, whose matrices are the identity modulo \(s\).

On the coordinates corresponding to \(x,z\), the three displayed automorphisms have matrices
\[
D=\begin{pmatrix}t&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A=E_{21}(s),\qquad
B=E_{12}(-s).
\tag{4}
\]
In particular,
\[
B_k=E_{12}(-s^{k+1}).
\tag{5}
\]

Balance determinants by adjoining a coordinate:
\[
g\longmapsto\operatorname{diag}(g,\det(g)^{-1}).
\]
The resulting matrices belong to the stable elementary group \(E(R)\), since
\(K_1(R)\cong\{\pm t^m\}\), with this isomorphism given by determinant.

We use the following consequence of Steinberg-symbol and local Hilbert-symbol theory.

**Detector lemma.** In the subgroup of \(E(R)\) consisting of matrices congruent to the identity modulo \(s\), the word
\[
[d,[a,\operatorname{ad}_d^{\,c-3}b]]
\]
does not belong to the \((c+1)\)-st lower central subgroup, where
\[
d=\operatorname{diag}(t,1,t^{-1}),\qquad
a=E_{21}(s),\qquad b=E_{12}(-s).
\]

Here are the details behind the lemma. Choose a prime \(p\) and a local field \(K\), with uniformizer \(\pi\), as follows.

* If an odd prime \(p\) divides \(c\), put \(k=c/p\) and use the Eisenstein polynomial
  \[
  \Phi_p(1+X^k).
  \]
* If \(c\) is a power of two, put \(d=c/4\) and use
  \[
  X^{2d}-2X^d+2.
  \]

In both cases the residue field is \(\mathbb F_p\), the field contains \(\mu_p\), and
\[
\frac{p\,v_K(p)}{p-1}=c.
\tag{6}
\]
In the quadratic case it also contains \(i\). Specialize \(t\) to \(1+\pi\).

Push the stable Steinberg extension of \(\operatorname{SL}(K)\) out through the \(p\)-th Hilbert symbol. This specialization defines a genuine homomorphism from \(E(R)\) into that cover: indeed,
\[
K_2(R)\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2
\]
is generated by \(\{-1,-1\}\) and \(\{-1,t\}\). Their Hilbert-symbol images vanish—by odd order when \(p\) is odd, and because \(-1\) is a square when \(p=2\).

Put \(U_r=1+\pi^r\mathcal O_K\). The local unit-pairing theorem gives
\[
(U_r,U_s)_p=1\quad(r+s>c),\qquad
U_{c+1}\subseteq K^{*p},
\]
and a nondegenerate critical pairing
\[
U_1/U_2\times U_{c-1}/U_c\longrightarrow\mu_p.
\]
Since the residue field is \(\mathbb F_p\), it follows that
\[
(1+\pi,1+\pi^{c-1})_p\ne1.
\tag{7}
\]

The usual congruence filtration lifts to the cover so that its quotient at depth \(c+1\) is nilpotent of class at most \(c\), while retaining the central \(\mu_p\). To check this, use full inverse images through depth \(c\), and above that depth use the canonical split root and torus lifts. Steinberg collection gives the commutator bounds: nonopposite roots have product parameters; torus–root commutators add depths; torus–torus discrepancies vanish when the depths sum to more than \(c\). Opposite-root discrepancies involve a symbol with first entry \(1+ab\); above depth \(c\), this entry is a \(p\)-th power. The deep split subgroup is therefore normal and has trivial intersection with \(\mu_p\).

Finally, evaluate the word in this nilpotent quotient. By (5), the inner commutator has opposite-root parameters
\[
a=s,\qquad b=-s^{c-2}.
\]
Its Gaussian decomposition has torus parameter
\[
1-ab=1+s^{c-1},
\]
and remaining root factors of depth at least \(c\). Commuting those root factors with \(d\) puts them in depth at least \(c+1\), so they disappear. The surviving torus commutator is
\[
(1+\pi,1+\pi^{c-1})_p^{\pm1},
\]
which is nontrivial by (7). The word thus has nontrivial image in a nilpotent group of class at most \(c\), proving the detector lemma.

Applying the lemma to the Alexander representation shows
\[
w_c\notin\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n).
\tag{8}
\]
The determinant-balancing coordinate makes this argument valid for every \(n\ge3\); it does not require a retraction from \(\operatorname{IA}_n\) to \(\operatorname{IA}_3\).

Combining (3) and (8) proves strictness for every \(n\ge3,\ c\ge3\). Together with the equality cases,
\[
\boxed{\mathcal D=\mathbb Z_{\ge3}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge3}.}
\]
